paras: The killing of Irene Hawkins took place on July 25, 1915, at the Savoy Hotel in Nashville, Tennessee, where Hawkins, a young Black chambermaid, was found dead in the alley beneath the window of a white guest's room. A coroner's jury charged the guest, E. J. Seymour, with raping and murdering her, and he was held in $2,500 bond. The case was carried only by Black weeklies, which used it to argue that crime was not confined to one race, and it prompted Black Nashville to raise money for the prosecution.

Hawkins worked as a chambermaid at the Savoy, a hotel on Seventh Avenue North in Nashville. Seymour was staying there and described himself as a traveling man, or salesman, from Chicago. According to testimony later given by another maid, Ada Stokes, he had tried a few days earlier to keep her in his room, and she escaped before he could lock the door. After that, Stokes said, she made sure he was out before she went in to clean.

On the afternoon of Sunday, July 25, Hawkins was seen in Seymour's room doing her work as chambermaid. Twenty minutes later her body was found, "bruised and mangled," in the alley directly under the window of his room. The Freeman's Nashville correspondent, who called it a "mysterious death," wrote that she had been summoned to Seymour's room and was beaten before being thrown from the window. Patrolman Carney found Seymour at the railroad station about to board a train for Chicago and arrested him.

The coroner opened an inquiry on Monday, and on Tuesday his jury returned a verdict charging Seymour with "violating the girl and then murdering her." According to the dispatch, the evidence showed that he had beaten and assaulted her before throwing her from the window. Seymour refused to answer the jury's questions, the Freeman correspondent reported. He was held by Murder Officers Jay Newsum and George Carter in bonds of $2,500, which the same correspondent said were soon furnished by friends.

Black Nashville organized to see the case pressed. A lawyer donated his services so that the case would receive a legal inquiry, and at a meeting called by the Negro Board of Trade about one hundred men "from all vocations of life" pledged money and voted to retain the best lawyer available to prosecute the assailant. No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The surviving coverage comes entirely from Black weeklies, and no white-newspaper account appears in it. A single Nashville dispatch, dated August 3 in the New York Age and August 10 elsewhere, ran in the Age on August 5, the Omaha Monitor on August 14, the Washington Bee on August 21, and the Cleveland Advocate on August 28 and again on September 4. The Baltimore Afro-American gave the case one sentence in an Easton, Maryland, column, notable for stating outright that Seymour was white.

Headlines carried the papers' argument. The Monitor titled the dispatch "Criminals Confined to No Particular Race," and the Bee put it on its front page as "White Brute Accused of Assaulting and Murdering Colored Girl in Hotel." The Cleveland Advocate headed its first printing "SEND FOR GEORGIA MOB!" In the Indianapolis Freeman, the Nashville correspondent Othello J. Hutchinson called Hawkins "this martyr of Negro womanhood" and praised the lawyer who took the case without fee.

The Freeman column's opening, badly garbled in print, gives the date as Sunday, July 27, and calls the victim "Irene Seymour, a 59-year-old woman," though its continuation names her Irene Hawkins. The syndicated dispatch, printed in four papers, gives Sunday, July 25, and describes Hawkins as "a colored girl," which fits its account of an inquest verdict on the following Tuesday.

reader.title: Killing of Irene Hawkins
bases: A single white guest, E. J. Seymour, was charged by a coroner's jury with raping and killing a Black hotel maid; no mob, band or officers took part in the killing (A1, A2, A5).

The syndicated Nashville dispatch (A1, A5, A6) and the independent account of the Freeman's Nashville correspondent (A3) agree on the death beneath Seymour's window, his arrest at the station and the $2,500 bond; the Afro-American brief (A2) adds that he was white.
